text: Last lesson ended on a real tension: five independently true findings on one architecture, and fixing all of them at once doesn't actually work, because some pull against each other. That's not a flaw in the framework — it's the single most important thing it teaches once the vocabulary sinks in. No real architecture optimizes every pillar at once.

Here's why. Every design decision spends a shared, finite budget — money, operational complexity, and acceptable risk — and the five pillars are competing claims on that same budget. Reliability spends money on redundancy. Cost optimization wants that money back. Operational excellence wants fewer moving parts to maintain. They cannot all win in the same design at the same time.

Take the reliability finding from last lesson and push on the fix: add active-active failover, a second region running production-capable infrastructure. That closes the reliability gap for real. But it roughly doubles steady-state compute cost, and it adds a failover runbook that has to actually be tested — an untested failover path isn't meaningfully different from having none at all. This is exactly the FinOps-versus-resilience tension from course ten, playing out as an architectural decision.

The failure mode to avoid is presenting a fix like this as if it were free. 'We'll add multi-region failover' sounds like a pure win until someone asks what it costs and who maintains it. A mature review names the tradeoff out loud and asks the real question: given this workload's revenue-per-minute of downtime, is that trade worth making? A payments API might say yes. A dashboard used twice a month almost certainly says no — and that's a legitimate, documented decision, not a shortcut.

Once you can name a tradeoff instead of hiding it, the next skill is spotting these same tensions just by looking at a diagram, before anyone says a word out loud. That's Lesson 4 — reading an architecture diagram the way an architect actually does.
